attachment.snippet:
1	---
2	name: authoring-agent-docs
3	description: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
4	---
5	
6	# Writing instruction files coding agents follow
7	
8	How to author the files an AI coding agent reads — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, an
9	agent or automation spec — so it follows them reliably. Grounded entirely in Anthropic's
10	published guidance; bracketed numbers cite the sources listed at the end.
11	
12	## Know what an instruction file is (and isn't)
13	
14	- Treat the file as context, not enforced configuration: the agent reads it and tries to
15	  follow it, with no guarantee of strict compliance. Anything that must happen every time
16	  (block a write, run a linter before commit) belongs in a deterministic hook instead. [1][2]
17	- Everything loaded at session start competes for a finite attention budget, and recall
18	  degrades as context grows ("context rot"). Aim for the smallest set of high-signal tokens
19	  that produces the behavior you want. [4]
20	- Keep the always-loaded file to facts that apply broadly in every session. Move multi-step
21	  procedures and sometimes-relevant domain knowledge into on-demand skills, and rules that
22	  matter for only part of the codebase into path-scoped rule files. [1][2]
23	
24	## Decide each line's right to exist
25	
26	- Include what the agent can't infer from code: build and test commands, style rules that
27	  differ from language defaults, repo etiquette (branch naming, PR conventions),
28	  project-specific architecture decisions, required env vars, non-obvious gotchas. [2]
29	- Exclude what it can figure out by reading code: standard conventions, file-by-file codebase
30	  descriptions, detailed API docs (link instead), frequently changing facts, and self-evident
31	  practices like "write clean code". [2]
32	- For each line, ask: "Would removing this cause the agent to make mistakes?" If not, cut it.
33	  Bloated instruction files cause the agent to ignore the instructions that matter. [2]
34	- Target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md; longer files consume more context and reduce
35	  adherence. Splitting into imports organizes but does not save context — imports still load
36	  at launch. [1]
37	
38	## Write each rule
39	
40	- Be concrete enough to verify: "Use 2-space indentation", not "Format code properly";
41	  "Run `npm test` before committing", not "Test your changes". [1]
42	- Apply the golden rule: show the instruction to a colleague with minimal context — if they'd
43	  be confused, the agent will be too. [3]
44	- State the motivation behind a rule, not just the rule; the model generalizes from the
45	  explanation. [3]
46	- Tell the agent what to do instead of what not to do: "write flowing prose paragraphs"
47	  steers better than "do not use markdown". [3]
48	- Use numbered steps when the order or completeness of steps matters. [3]
49	- Prefer a few (3–5) diverse, canonical examples over a laundry list of edge-case rules, and
50	  wrap them in `<example>` tags so they can't be mistaken for instructions. [3][4]
51	- Pitch rules at the right altitude: specific enough to guide behavior, flexible enough to
52	  leave the model strong heuristics — avoiding both brittle hardcoded if-then logic and vague
53	  guidance that assumes shared context. [4]
54	- Reserve emphasis ("IMPORTANT", "YOU MUST") for tuning adherence on rules that slip. [2]
55	
56	## Structure the file
57	
58	- Group related rules under markdown headers and bullets; the agent scans structure the way
59	  readers do, and organized sections are easier to follow than dense paragraphs. [1]
60	- Separate content types — background, instructions, tool guidance, output format — into
61	  distinct sections with consistent, descriptive names (Markdown headers or XML tags). [3][4]
62	- Make a task spec self-contained: name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out
63	  of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step that proves the work. [2]
64	- Give the agent a check it can run — a test suite, build exit code, linter, or comparison
65	  script. Without one, "looks done" is its only stopping signal. [2]
66	
67	## Maintain it like code
68	
69	- Start minimal and add rules in response to observed failures: the agent makes the same
70	  mistake a second time, a review catches something it should have known, or you retype last
71	  session's correction. [1][4]
72	- Test edits by observing whether behavior actually shifts. If a rule keeps being ignored,
73	  the file is probably too long and the rule is lost in the noise. [2]
74	- Remove contradictions: if two rules conflict — including across nested or imported files —
75	  the agent may pick one arbitrarily. [1]
76	- Prune regularly. If the agent already behaves correctly without a rule, delete it or
77	  convert it to a hook. Check the file into version control so the team contributes and it
78	  compounds in value. [2]
79	- When a practice is withdrawn, rewrite the docs that taught it into the **current** rule in the
80	  present tense — never leave a passage narrating what used to be done and why it stopped. A reader
81	  who never knew the practice doesn't need to be taught it in order to be told the rule, and
82	  describing a withdrawn technique is how it keeps getting rediscovered; the history belongs to the
83	  commit that removed it. This bans narrating a *superseded* way of working, not evidence — measured
84	  costs that argue a live rule is worth its space stay. And retiring a practice is not the moment to
85	  install a guard against it: a check earns its place from a mistake that repeats, not from the
86	  deletion that prompted it.
